newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil debt outlook stable, but worrisome.
newsitem.headline: Brazil debt outlook stable, but worrisome.

text.p: Brazil's stock of internal debt is growing at manageable levels, but policy-makers will have to work much harder in the future to keep it under control, economic analysts said.

"The (debt) trend is good as far as interest rates and dollar inflows are concerned. But when you see what we are facing, the government is going to have to do a lot more," said the chief economist at an international bank in Brazil who requested anonymity.

Falling domestic interest rates and fewer net dollar inflows, which force the government to issue bonds to soak up the excess liquidity, have helped keep domestic debt buildup in check over the past few months.
But a number of worrying factors on the horizon threaten to push up Brazil's current debt-to-gross domestic product ratio of 34 percent.

First, economists fear the federal government's fragile committment to fiscal restraint will be further pressured by October municipal elections and President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's bid to push a re-election amendment through Congress.

Second, some 40 billion reais in mortgage debt under a housing program remains to be securitized. Full recognition of the debt would add about seven percentage points to the debt-to-GDP ratio, economists say.
In addition, the government's aid program for private and state banks could add close to 30 billion reais to the debt stock.
All told, the additions could push Brazil's total public debt, now at 240 billion reais, over the 300 billion mark in the not-too-distant future.

The country's current debt-to-GDP ratio is small when compared to Belgium, Italy or Canada, whose ratios range from 80 percent to over 100 percent. But a 34 percent ratio is worrisome for a speculative- grade country like Brazil, economists say.

Last week International Monetary Fund (IMF) and Inter-American Development officials expressed concern about Brazil's domestic debt. They made their comments during a seminar on public finances in Brasilia.
IMF fiscal affairs director Vitor Tanzi called the results of an IMF study on Brazil's debt outlook "worrisome" and said the country had to slow the pace of its debt buildup.
But unlike its cash-strapped neighbor Argentina, whose policy-makers are forever scrambling to meet IMF targets, Brazil is sitting atop some $60 billion in foreign reserves.
As a result, Brazil does not rely on IMF aid packages and it has adopted a "We'll keep it in mind" attitude to suggestions it move faster on the fiscal and debt front.
"We don't need any Dr. Tanzis coming to warn us (about debt and fiscal matters)," Central Bank International Affairs Director Gustavo Franco said after the seminar.
Franco said Brazil's debt-to-GDP ratio could rise to 36 percent or 37 percent this year but that it would remain under control.
Economists are not so optimistic. But they did say Brazil could do a number of things to avoid a sharp hike in debt.
For example, rather than posting all of the 40 billion reais in mortgage debt under a housing program, the government could tack it on gradually.

"We don't know exactly how they are going to post it. But I don't think they would do it all at once, which would cause a dramatic rise in the debt stock," said Tomas Malaga, an economist at Brazilian bank Unibanco.
Economists also said the government would have to speed up its privatization drive and move faster on constitutional reform to reduce pressure on public accounts.
--Sao Paulo newsroom, 5511 232-4411
